body_markdown:
In 2006, you could buy a decent 1971 Ford Bronco for well under $10,000. And plenty of people did, not because they were necessarily trying to get ahead of the market, but more likely because they just liked first-generation Broncos. I still wince at the memory of turning down one with 30,000 miles in 2005 for $11K, but that’s my cross to bear. Today, that same ’71 transacts[around $50,000](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/bronco/1971/1971-ford-bronco-base?id=aCn1I000000D4idSAC) in merely “good” condition. And the dudes who bought their early Broncos 20 years ago now get treated like oracles each weekend at cars and coffee.


Ford


The Bronco valuation story isn’t all slam-dunks, though, and there have been some recent corrections. If you bought that same ’71 in early 2022, near the very top of the market, 20% of your investment disappeared like[Keyser Söze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyser_S%C3%B6ze) in the last four years. The only thing that was different was the date on the check.


The vintage truck market just finished teaching its second big lesson in five years. The first lesson was that unglamorous, utilitarian 4x4s can appreciate like Italian sports cars. The second was that they can correct like them, too. The market didn’t collapse or anything, but it did correct. And if you study the latest Hagerty Price Guide data closely, you can see that it has[started to rise again](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-indexes-trend-upwards-despite-a-picky-market/) , if only slightly.


## Why the Demand Never Left


Toyota


Strip out the past few years of noise, and the 20-year picture remains astonishing. Well, it might not be so astonishing for boomers who watched Hemi ’Cudas go stratospheric. But it’s astonishing for a millennial like me who’s seeing their uncle’s farm truck somehow go blue-chip.


A good-condition first-gen Bronco is up more than 400% this century. Amazingly, rougher examples have appreciated even faster. FJ40 Land Cruisers that traded in the mid-$20,000s in the late aughts have sent their best examples into six figures.


The reason is[a generational handoff](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/how-the-vintage-truck-market-got-so-big/comment-page-2/) . There is a[financial handoff](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/data-driven/the-great-car-transfer-has-begun/) underway, but there’s also been a shift in tastes. Some of the buyers who spent decades chasing Corvettes and muscle cars are aging out of the hobby. Many of the folks replacing them didn’t grow up dreaming about lacquer paint and numbers-matching big-blocks. They, like me, grew up in the third row of the family 4×4. They came of age with SUVs as the dominant car of their era. And they are buying accordingly.


“Vintage 4×4 demand is being fueled primarily by Gen X enthusiasts, with some strong input from millennials,” says Greg Ingold, Senior Manager of Vehicle Valuation at Hagerty. Fifteen years ago, he notes, baby boomers were the clear drivers of collecting habits. The change in the market has come right on the heels of younger enthusiasts entering it.


## The Party—and the Hangover


Paul Mehaffey


That demand recently hit a peak in the 2020–22 frenzy, when folks had cheap money and a lot of time on their hands to refresh auction sites. It was a perfect recipe, and it sent the whole segment (along with just about the entire classic market) vertical. Then, starting in late 2022, the market flinched. Per the current Hagerty Price Guide, a[good-condition Grand Wagoneer](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jeep/grand_wagoneer/1986/1986-jeep-grand_wagoneer-base?id=aCn1I000000CqVVSA0&timeframe=5Y) is down more than 26% over three years. An[FJ60 Land Cruiser](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/toyota/land_cruiser/1982/1982-toyota-land_cruiser-fj60?id=aCn1I000000DTEsSAO) is off 20%. Even Scout IIs, my beloved orphans,[slid about 10%.](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/international_(ihc)/scout_ii/1973/1973-international_(ihc)-scout_ii-base?id=aCn1I000000D66QSAS) If you bought at the top, none of this is news to you. Sorry to rub it in.


Though often painful if you get bit by one, corrections can be clarifying; they shake out the speculators and leave the people who actually wanted the truck for the long haul sitting pretty. What’s more, they reset entry prices to levels the segment hasn’t seen since before the madness. This brings us to what the data started doing this year. And, pardon my editorializing, it’s heartening.


## The Turn


I don’t mean to sound all Occupy Wall Street-y, but markets tend to recover from the top down. That is exactly the order in which the collector-truck market is turning. The FJ40, long the segment’s blue chip, never really dived, and[some models](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/toyota/land_cruiser/1980/1980-toyota-land_cruiser-fj40v?id=aCn1I000000CswwSAC) are up 23% over three years and 8.2% in the past year alone.


The Grand Wagoneer, which fell hardest, is, oddly enough, snapping back sharpest: up almost 9% on the year. The Scout II has crept back to positive. And the Bronco has stopped falling. It’s dead flat for the past quarter, after three years of downfall.


The overall pattern matters more than any single number. The market has found its footing. The most established nameplate has firmed up first. And that strength spreads outward from there.


Ingold sees it too, but with a data wonk’s caution. “I would say there is a recovery going on with these segment leaders,” he says. Whether the love trickles down to the corners of the market that haven’t moved yet is harder to call, but, he adds, “I wouldn’t count it out.”


That said, there are two trucks the recovery hasn’t reached yet.


## Where the Value Is Hiding


Toyota


The FJ60 is the “buy” of the segment right now. I say that as a man with no FJ60 to sell you. It is the FJ40’s direct successor, and it has traced the 40’s demand curve, but has always been a few years behind. It’s currently down 20% over three years and 15% over the past year, with a good-condition value around $24,800. If the FJ40 has turned, history says the 60 will follow.


After digging into the numbers, I was also shocked to discover that the whole cycle skipped the 1969–91 K10 Chevy Blazer. It barely bubbled and barely corrected. It’s[off just 3.1%](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/k10_blazer/1975/1975-chevrolet-k10_blazer-cheyenne?id=aCn1I000000D97jSAC) over three years and flat everywhere else, and a good ’75 Cheyenne with a 350 V-8 is sitting around $24,900 right now. Square-body fever has been spreading outward from the pickups for years; the Blazer is the same truck, with a lid on it, and arguably more useful because it has a backseat. Why folks are sleeping on these is beyond me.


Chevrolet


Ingold’s own early-curve picks sit a generation newer still. “I strongly believe that the next wave of collectible trucks is coming,” he says, pointing to the 1990s and early 2000s. These are the GMT400-era GM trucks, which he says “still have plenty of room to grow.” There’s also the GMT800 that followed them, 10th-generation Ford F-Series, second-gen Dodge Rams, and the Land Cruisers and 4Runners of the same era.


And below all of this sits the driver-tier I covered in the recent *[5 Collector Trucks You Can Drive Daily for $15K](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/5-collector-trucks-you-can-drive-daily-for-15k/)* piece: Comanches, FJ80s, OBS pickups, honest trucks at used-sedan money. That story hasn’t changed. If anything, the correction above them makes those trucks look even smarter. Note the overlap, too: The OBS Chevy in that piece is Ingold’s GMT400.


## Nobody Rings a Bell


The old market saying holds that nobody rings a bell at the bottom. But a blue chip going green after a three-year washout is about as close to a bell as this hobby ever gets.


The folks who bought the ’71 Bronco in 2006 weren’t geniuses. They just liked trucks, bought one they wanted to drive, and let 20 years happen. That exact move is available again, one tier down, at post-correction prices.


I’m not a financial adviser. I’m a guy with an orphan Scout Traveler in his dad’s barn and an FJ80 Land Cruiser that has stranded him on the highway. But if you’ve been waiting for the smart moment to buy the old truck you actually want, it might be now.
